sentences.text: The genus name Dinevenator combines a tribute to the Diné people with the Latin word for hunter.
Robert M. Sullivan described the fossil in 2006 after it was recovered in the summer of 2005 from the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico.
The specimen was catalogued as SMP VP-1955 at the State Museum of Pennsylvania and was initially assigned to Saurornitholestes robustus.
In 2012 Alan H. Turner regarded the taxon as a nomen dubium, a status later revised in 2014 when David C. Evans concluded it represented an indeterminate troodontid unrelated to Saurornitholestes.
A 2026 study by Hector E. Rivera-Sylva and colleagues tentatively placed the specimen in the genus Xenovenator as X.? robustus.
Earlier work had linked the specimen to the genera Saurornitholestes and Xenovenator.
Phylogenetic analysis recovered Dinevenator robustus as the most basal member of a clade of robust troodontins, sister to Albertavenator curriei and Xenovenator espinosai.
Dinevenator lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Its type locality is the Kirtland Formation, a Late Cretaceous deposit in New Mexico, United States.
The animal is known from this formation as an extinct troodontid theropod.
Paleontologists have debated whether the taxon is a nomen dubium or an indeterminate troodontid not belonging to Saurornitholestes.
